title: Elihu Enters: The Young Man Must Speak
summary: Job's three friends fall silent, and a new speaker appears: Elihu, a younger man who has been listening. He is angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and angry with the friends for condemning Job without answering him. He explains that he waited out of respect for age, but that understanding comes from God's spirit, not from years. Now he is so full of words that he must speak, and he promises to show no partiality.
story: Job has completed his defense and signed it, demanding that God answer (31:35-37). The reader expects God to speak next. Instead, a character never mentioned before steps forward. Elihu's speeches fill six chapters (32 to 37), and no one interrupts or answers him. This chapter is his introduction, explaining why he is speaking at all. His arrival creates suspense and delay: Job has called for God, and he gets another human voice instead. Elihu will argue that God speaks to people through dreams and suffering (chapter 33), defend God's justice (chapters 34 and 35), and describe God's majesty in a storm (chapters 36 and 37), which leads directly into God's own speech from the whirlwind in chapter 38.
historical:
Elihu is introduced with more genealogical detail than anyone else in the book: son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram (verse 2). Buz is the name of a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother (Genesis 22:21), whose brother Uz shares a name with Job's homeland. Jeremiah 25:23 lists Buz with Dedan and Tema, peoples of northern Arabia. These links place Elihu among the peoples east of Israel, in the same world as Job and his friends. The name Elihu means He is my God, and it is also borne by other people in the Old Testament. Nothing is known about this Elihu outside this book, and he is not mentioned in the prologue or the epilogue.

The prose introduction in verses 1-5 is the first narrative since chapter 2, apart from the short speaker headings. It explains the situation in a way the poetry alone could not: the friends have stopped because Job was righteous in his own eyes (verse 1), and Elihu has been waiting because he was younger.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, as in most traditional societies, age was closely linked to wisdom. The elders sat at the gate and gave counsel, and the young were expected to listen before they spoke. Eliphaz had appealed to this very principle (15:10). Elihu honors it at first, saying that age should speak and many years should teach wisdom (verse 7), but then he challenges it: understanding comes from the breath of the Almighty (verse 8), which can be given to the young as well as the old.

Elihu's image of his own condition (verse 19) comes from winemaking. New wine was stored in skins made from goat hides, and as it fermented, the gas expanded; if the skin had no vent, it could burst. Jesus used the same practice in his saying about new wine and old wineskins (Mark 2:22). Elihu says he is like a sealed wineskin, so full of words that he must speak or burst.
literary: The chapter begins with a prose introduction (verses 1-5) that repeats one idea four times: Elihu's anger was kindled, against Job (verse 2), against the friends (verse 3), and again when he saw they had no answer (verse 5). Then the poetry begins (verses 6-22), with Elihu's long justification for speaking. It is unusually self-referential: he talks at length about his own youth, his waiting, his fullness of words, and his impartiality before saying anything about Job's case. Some readers find this humorous or pompous, a young man clearing his throat for sixteen verses; others see it as the proper courtesy of a younger man addressing elders. The repeated phrase what I know (verses 6, 10, 17) and the vivid image of the bursting wineskin give the speech its energy. There is also a small textual question in verse 3: an ancient Jewish scribal tradition lists this verse among places where scribes altered wording out of reverence, suggesting that the original may have said the friends had condemned God, not Job.

outline.t: The friends fall silent, and Elihu grows angry
Wisdom comes from God's spirit, not from age
The friends have failed to answer Job
Full of words, Elihu must speak without partiality

doctrines.note: Elihu says that it is the spirit in a person, the breath of the Almighty, that gives understanding (verse 8). Wisdom is ultimately a gift of God, not a product of age or experience. The Bible elsewhere connects wisdom closely with the work of God's Spirit.

Elihu challenges the assumption that wisdom always belongs to the old. Scripture honors the wisdom of age, but it also shows God giving understanding to the young, such as Joseph, Samuel, and Daniel. Wisdom is measured by its source and its truth, not by the speaker's years.

Elihu's claim that God's breath gives understanding raises the question of how God speaks. In the chapters ahead, Elihu will argue that God speaks in more ways than Job has recognized, through dreams and through suffering itself.

words.note: Elihu, meaning He is my God. The name appears four times in the Hebrew text of this chapter. It is also carried by several other people in the Old Testament. The name fits his role as a defender of God's justice.

Aph, nose, and by extension anger, from the flaring of the nostrils. The phrase his anger was kindled, literally his nose burned, appears four times in verses 2-5. Elihu's entrance is marked by anger, against Job for justifying himself and against the friends for failing to answer him.

Ruach, spirit, breath, or wind. In verse 8 Elihu says there is a spirit in a man that gives him understanding, and in verse 18 his spirit within him compels him to speak. The word ties the human spirit to the breath of God that gave life to the first man.

Kanah, to give a flattering title or to address with honorifics. Elihu uses it twice in verses 21-22, promising not to flatter anyone. In ancient speech, addressing someone with elaborate titles was a sign of respect, but Elihu says it would be dishonest here.

christ: Elihu's claim that understanding comes not from age but from the breath of the Almighty has a thematic echo in the story of Jesus. When Jesus was twelve years old, he sat among the teachers in the temple, listening and asking questions, and all who heard him were amazed at his understanding (Luke 2:46-47). Later, people asked how he knew so much without formal study (John 7:15), and he answered that his teaching came from the one who sent him. The New Testament also promises that the Spirit gives wisdom to believers regardless of age or status (Acts 2:17, drawing on Joel 2:28). None of this is predicted in Job 32. Elihu is a flawed and sometimes self-important speaker. But his insistence that wisdom is a gift of God's Spirit points toward a truth fulfilled in Christ and in the church.

hard.q: Is Elihu a wise voice or another failed comforter?
hard.a: Interpreters have long disagreed. Some see Elihu as a positive figure who corrects both Job and the friends and prepares the way for God's speeches. They note that he offers a new idea, that suffering can be a form of God's discipline and warning, and that God does not rebuke him at the end of the book (42:7-9 mentions only the three friends). Others see him as a pompous young man who repeats the friends' arguments at greater length; they point to his long self-introduction, his anger, and the fact that God, when he speaks, ignores Elihu entirely. Still others think the Elihu speeches were added to the book later, noting that he is not mentioned in the prologue or epilogue and that his style differs from the rest. A fourth view sees him as deliberately ambiguous, a character whose partial truth and partial arrogance are part of the book's design. The text itself does not settle the question, and readers should weigh his words carefully, as they would any human speaker in Job.

questions: Elihu waited to speak out of respect for his elders. When is it wise to wait before speaking, and when does silence become a failure?
Elihu says wisdom comes from God's spirit, not from age. How should the young and the old learn from each other?
Elihu is angry with Job and with the friends. When have you been so sure you were right that you could not wait to speak? What happened?
